parts.text:
Many marine organisms can become attached to hard surfaces such as rocks or the surfaces
of ships. These organisms are known as fouling organisms.
The larva of the acorn barnacle, Amphibalanus amphitrite, is an example of a fouling
organism. One of these barnacle larvae is shown in Fig. 3.1.
magnification ×160
Fig. 3.1
The larvae of A. amphitrite use a protein to attach themselves to the surfaces of ships.
It is expensive to remove fouling organisms from ships. Scientists have developed substances
to prevent the attachment of larvae. However, some of these substances are toxic and have
been responsible for a decrease in marine biodiversity.
Scientists investigated the effect of using an immobilised protease, subtilisin A, to prevent the
attachment of the larvae of A. amphitrite to surfaces.
The scientists used 4 different concentrations of subtilisin A which had been immobilised onto
the surface of a polymer film. As a control they used denatured subtilisin A immobilised onto
the surface of the same polymer. Glass slides were also used as a control.
* 0000800000009 * DFD

• 4 tanks, each with a polymer surface and a different concentration of immobilised
subtilisin A

• 1 tank with glass slides instead of a polymer surface.
The number of larvae that attached to the different surfaces in the tanks was counted after
